question: In the ward, what do we mean by an 'adverse event'?

options.A: Harm caused by medical management rather than the disease
options.B: An unavoidable symptom of a natural disease process
options.C: Any emotional stress a patient feels before surgery
options.D: A patient refusing to take prescribed hospital medications

explanation: Spot on! An adverse event means the patient got hurt because of the care or treatment given, not because of their sickness itself. You'll master these safety terms in no time! [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h1)

question: Why is it important for nurses to figure out if a patient's worsening condition is from the disease or from medical care?

options.A: To prove that doctors are always responsible for clinical outcomes
options.B: To determine if the injury resulted from care management or the illness
options.C: To ensure the hospital avoids paying any financial compensation
options.D: To decide which patients need emergency psychological counseling

explanation: Exactly! We need to know if the problem came naturally from the illness or if something in our care caused it, so we can fix our processes and help the patient better. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h1)

question: What happens when a nurse falls into 'confirmation bias' during clinical assessment?

options.A: Forgetting to check vital signs because of a sudden emergency
options.B: Trusting equipment alarms even when they are making false noises
options.C: Blaming a coworker for a mistake you made during a procedure
options.D: Looking only for signs that prove your first guess and ignoring others

explanation: You got it! Confirmation bias is when our brain only looks for clues that match our very first thought about what is wrong, while ignoring other important signs. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h2)

question: A maternity nurse ignores a fetal monitor beep because too many false alarms sounded earlier. What is this called?
explanation: Well done! When machines beep too often for nothing, we get 'alert fatigue' and might sadly miss the one time the alarm is actually saving a life. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h2)

question: In the famous 'Swiss Cheese Model' of patient safety, what do the holes in the cheese represent?

options.A: The specific mistakes made by an individual nurse
options.B: Broken equipment waiting for replacement parts
options.C: Weaknesses and flaws in hospital safety defenses
options.D: Gaps in the patient's personal medical history

explanation: Spot on! Each slice of cheese is a safety layer, and the holes are the gaps or weaknesses. An error happens when all the holes line up at once. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h3)

question: Why is it usually unhelpful to just punish a nurse after a mistake happens on the ward?

options.A: It stops other staff members from documenting patient care properly
options.B: It ignores the underlying system flaws that allowed the error to happen
options.C: It makes the nurse work faster during the next emergency shift
options.D: It increases the budget available for buying new medical equipment

explanation: Exactly! Blaming just one person doesn't fix a broken system. To keep patients safe, we have to fix the root causes so the same mistake doesn't happen again. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h3)

question: When handing over patients, what does the SBAR communication tool stand for?
explanation: You nailed it! SBAR keeps our shift handovers clear, quick, and professional so nothing important gets missed. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h4)

question: A junior nurse sees a mother bleeding heavily after birth but stays quiet because she is scared of the senior doctor. What kind of barrier is this?
explanation: Spot on. Strict hospital ranks can make junior staff too intimidated to speak up. Patient safety means every voice matters, no matter your rank! [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h4)

question: Which of these is a common technology-related cause of patient harm in the hospital?

options.A: Confusing device interfaces and poor equipment maintenance
options.B: Patients refusing to take prescribed oral vitamins
options.C: Too many nurses practicing basic clinical hand hygiene
options.D: Doctors writing clear prescriptions in paper charts

explanation: Correct! When medical gadgets have confusing screens or aren't serviced well, it leads to mistakes that can harm patients. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h5)

question: Why is it dangerous to rely 100% on a machine monitor without doing a physical check on your patient?

options.A: It prevents the nurse from writing notes in the electronic health record system
options.B: The hospital will charge the patient extra fees for electronic monitoring services
options.C: It always causes the patient to develop severe anxiety and panic attacks
options.D: The machine might malfunction or display data that does not match the patient's actual condition

explanation: You got it! Machines can glitch or give false readings. Your eyes, hands, and clinical judgment as a nurse are always the best safeguard. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h5)

question: What do we call a 'near miss' in the hospital?

options.A: An error that is caught before it reaches or harms the patient
options.B: A patient complaint about long waiting times at the clinic
options.C: A minor side effect of a drug that was expected by the doctor
options.D: An adverse event that causes permanent physical disability

explanation: Spot on! A near miss is a lucky save where a mistake almost happened, but someone caught it right on time before the patient got hurt. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h6)

question: Why should nurses always report near misses, even though no patient was hurt?

options.A: They reveal hidden system flaws that can be fixed before a real injury happens
options.B: They allow the hospital administration to discipline careless workers
options.C: They guarantee that the hospital will receive extra government funding
options.D: They reduce the total number of patients admitted to the maternity ward

explanation: Brilliant! Reporting near misses gives us warning signs so we can fix hidden dangers before they turn into real tragedies. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h6)

question: Which of these practices helps stop clinical errors during tricky or high-risk procedures?

options.A: Discouraging nurses from reporting small near misses
options.B: Using standardized checklists and safety protocols
options.C: Allowing staff to work longer shifts without taking breaks
options.D: Removing all electronic monitoring devices from the ward

explanation: You nailed it! Checklists make sure we never skip critical steps, keeping both patients and busy nurses safe. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h7)

question: What is the main goal of modern patient safety design in healthcare?

options.A: To make doing the right thing easy and mistakes difficult
options.B: To eliminate all forms of human emotion from clinical work
options.C: To hide medical errors from patients and their families
options.D: To punish nurses severely whenever an adverse event occurs

explanation: Spot on! Good hospital design sets up simple workflows that naturally guide us to do the right thing every time. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h7)
